title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
hook: Jesus steps into the line of sinners, the sky opens, a voice says beloved

segments.voice: Yesterday: metanoia, a turning around, and John's voice in the desert clearing the road for someone greater.

A long line at the river. Everyone in it is there for the same reason: they've done things they regret, and they want to turn around. A tax man. A soldier. A woman who hasn't spoken to her sister in years. Nobody in that line is showing off. Then a carpenter from Nazareth steps in and waits his turn like everybody else. When he reaches the front, John looks at him and stops. He knows who this is, and he tries to refuse.
screen: `A LINE OF PEOPLE WITH REGRETS.` → `A CARPENTER STEPS INTO LINE.` → `JOHN TRIES TO REFUSE.`

segments.voice: John's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?" It's backward, he means: you should be baptizing me. Jesus answers that it is fitting, for now, to fulfill all justice, and John lets him come down into the river. Why get in line at all? Christians have asked that for two thousand years. The Church's answer: not for his own sins. He was standing where sinners stand, on purpose, in the water with them. Then the story opens up. As he comes out, Matthew says, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him. And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. Before a single miracle, sermon, follower or healing, he's already beloved. The Church reads the scene as a window onto the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. The feast of the Baptism of the Lord closes the Christmas season, and it's the first of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary. Catholics hear their own baptism in it too: the Catechism teaches that baptism makes a person an adopted child of God. That's why there's holy water at the church door. People dip their fingers and make the sign of the cross on the way in, remembering the water they came through.
screen: `JOHN: YOU SHOULD BAPTIZE ME.` · `HE STANDS WHERE SINNERS STAND.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE DOES ANYTHING.` · `HOLY WATER AT THE CHURCH DOOR.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: If you can, touch a little water from a glass or a tap, and feel how cool or warm it is; a Catholic might make the sign of the cross, as at the church door; if not, just let the water be water. Then sit, and let one sentence rest on you: loved, before doing anything.
The baptism. Jesus steps into the river with sinners, and a voice from heaven calls him beloved.
Your line: you are the beloved. Loved first, before any of the day's work. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that ends the Christmas season, pray it as the first Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and bless themselves with holy water on entering a church as a reminder of their own baptism.

original.note: Greek: beloved, dearly loved. From agapē, love. The word the voice from heaven uses.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus got baptized to wash off his sins.
what it means: the Church teaches he had no sins to wash. he got in line to stand where sinners stand, and heard he was beloved.
what a scholar hears: Christians read the scene as a picture of the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 3:14 and 3:17 given from memory; confirm.
The hook's people in line (a tax man, a soldier) come from Luke 3:12–14, not Matthew; the 'woman estranged from her sister' is illustrative. Confirm this is acceptable as scene-setting.
'He wasn't there for his own sins': Catholic teaching that Jesus was sinless and accepted baptism in solidarity with sinners (CCC 536). Confirm phrasing.
CCC 1265: baptism makes the neophyte an adopted son of God; paraphrased.
Baptism of the Lord ends the Christmas season in the Roman calendar; first Luminous Mystery (John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae, 2002). Confirm.
Holy water at church doors as a reminder of baptism: describes common practice; confirm.
